article.title: When AI Makes Work Faster but Not Necessarily Better
article.framework: Task Decomposition → AI Speed-Up → Bottleneck Shift → Verification Cost → System-Level Outcome
article.coreIdea: AI can dramatically accelerate one step of a workflow without producing an equally large improvement in total productivity. The key is to identify where the bottleneck moves, how verification costs change, and whether faster output creates more useful work or simply more work to review.
article.body:
A worker opens an AI assistant and receives a polished draft in seconds. A programmer generates code that would have taken an hour to type. A marketing team produces twenty campaign ideas before lunch. From examples like these, it is tempting to conclude that artificial intelligence simply makes knowledge work faster. Sometimes it does. But speed at one stage of a process is not the same as productivity across the whole system.

Imagine a five-step workflow: gather information, create a first draft, check accuracy, obtain approval, and implement the result. If AI cuts drafting time from sixty minutes to six, that is an impressive reduction for one task. Yet if the other stages still take three hours, total completion time falls much less. Its system-level effect depends on where difficulty remains.

This is a bottleneck problem. A bottleneck is the part of a system that most strongly limits overall output. When technology removes one bottleneck, another often becomes more important. Faster drafting may make fact-checking the new constraint. Faster coding may increase the amount of code waiting for review. Faster design generation may shift scarce attention toward choosing among alternatives.

The distinction resembles stock and flow. AI can increase the flow of drafts, images, analyses, or code, but the stock of human attention may not increase at the same rate. If people must inspect every output before it affects customers, financial decisions, or software systems, review capacity becomes scarce. More production upstream can create congestion downstream.

This is why “time saved” is surprisingly difficult to measure. Suppose an employee previously spent two hours writing a report and now spends thirty minutes generating and editing it with AI. Did the organization gain ninety minutes of productive capacity? Perhaps. But the employee might use that time to create a longer report, check more sources, or respond to more requests. Total workload may still expand.

A tool can reduce labor required for a specific activity, but productivity at the organizational level depends on complementary changes. Teams may need new processes, clearer responsibilities, better data, or different approval rules before the technological gain becomes fully useful.

Verification is one important complement. Generative AI can produce fluent output even when parts of it are wrong. Fluency lowers the friction of creation, but it does not eliminate the need for judgment. In some settings, checking a plausible-looking answer can be harder than creating a simple answer from scratch because the reviewer must identify hidden errors rather than obvious missing content.

This creates a verification burden. The faster a system generates outputs, the more important it becomes to decide which outputs require careful checking and who is responsible for that checking. If verification is equally intensive for every AI-generated item, organizations may move work rather than remove it.

Risk changes the calculation. A minor error in an internal brainstorming document may be harmless. The same error in a legal filing, financial model, or production codebase can be expensive. The appropriate level of verification should therefore depend on consequence, not merely on whether AI was used.

This connects to #52's Process-Outcome Split. A successful AI-generated answer does not prove that a workflow is reliable, just as one lucky investment does not prove that the decision process was sound. Reliability must be evaluated across repeated cases. A system that is correct 95 percent of the time may be excellent for low-stakes ideation and unacceptable where the remaining 5 percent can cause severe harm.

Measurement can also be distorted by proxy targets. If a company evaluates AI adoption by counting how many documents employees produce, workers may generate more documents. But document volume is only a proxy for useful output. If nobody reads the additional material, the measured productivity gain may represent activity rather than value.

A better metric starts closer to the objective. For customer support, the goal may be problems resolved accurately and quickly, not messages written. For software development, it may be reliable features delivered, not lines of code generated. For research, it may be useful conclusions supported by evidence, not pages summarized. AI changes intermediate quantities easily, so measurement should move toward final value.

There are second-order effects too. When producing a first draft becomes cheap, people may attempt projects that previously seemed too expensive. A small business can test more advertisements. A student can ask for more explanations. A programmer can prototype several approaches. Lower costs can encourage useful experimentation.

But cheaper generation can also create abundance problems. If everyone can produce presentations, proposals, emails, images, and reports at much lower cost, recipients face more material competing for the same attention. What is cheap for the sender may become expensive for the receiver. The bottleneck shifts from creation to selection.

The same principle applies to expertise. AI may reduce the value of remembering routine information while increasing the value of asking good questions, evaluating evidence, noticing unusual cases, and understanding context. Skills are not simply replaced; their relative scarcity changes. When basic production becomes abundant, judgment can become more valuable.

There is also a feedback issue. Junior workers often learn by doing tasks that experts later review. If AI performs much of the first-pass work, juniors may become faster immediately but receive less practice constructing solutions themselves. In the short term, output rises. In the long term, the pipeline that creates future expertise could weaken unless training is redesigned.

This does not mean organizations should preserve inefficient work merely for practice. It means automation has both first-order and second-order effects. The first-order effect is obvious: a task becomes faster. The second-order questions are harder: Where does the bottleneck move? What happens to learning? Does review capacity keep up? Does the organization produce more value or simply more artifacts?

Today's transferable tool is the Bottleneck Shift Test. Start by decomposing a workflow into stages. Identify the current constraint. Then ask which stage AI accelerates, what new volume that creates, and which downstream stage becomes scarce. Finally, measure the outcome at the level of the real objective rather than the easiest intermediate metric.

If AI helps a team write ten proposals instead of three, do not stop at “proposal output increased.” Ask whether managers can review ten proposals, whether customers receive better offers, whether win rates change, and whether the extra options improve decisions. The mechanism still needs to be visible.

This perspective prevents two extreme conclusions. One is that AI productivity gains are imaginary because humans still need to check the work. The other is that a tenfold speed-up in one task automatically creates a tenfold productivity gain. Both ignore the system around the task.

Technology often changes the location of scarcity rather than eliminating scarcity itself. Calculators reduced the scarcity of arithmetic. Search engines reduced the scarcity of accessible information. Generative AI reduces the scarcity of first drafts and plausible outputs. As each constraint becomes cheaper, another resource—attention, verification, trust, coordination, or judgment—can become relatively more valuable.

So the right question is not simply, “How much faster can AI do this task?” It is, “What happens to the entire workflow when this task becomes cheap?” That shift from task-level speed to system-level productivity is essential for understanding where AI creates durable value.
article.summaryZh:
今天讨论一个很容易被“AI 快了十倍”掩盖的问题：task-level speed-up 不等于 system-level productivity gain。核心链条是 Task Decomposition → AI Speed-Up → Bottleneck Shift → Verification Cost → System-Level Outcome。AI 增加 drafts/code/images 的 flow，却不一定同步增加 human attention 这个稀缺 stock，所以 creation 变便宜后，scarcity 往往移动到 review、selection、trust 或 judgment。

这接回 friction：降低 creation friction 能促进 experimentation，但旧 friction 也可能承担过滤低价值输出的作用；过滤消失后，系统需要在别处建立 selective friction。接 #52 Process-Outcome Split：一次 AI 输出正确不证明 workflow reliable，可靠性必须跨 repeated cases 测量。也接 measurement：documents produced、lines of code 等只是 intermediate metrics，真正目标应靠近 problems solved、reliable features delivered、useful conclusions 等 final value。

文章还加入 second-order effect：如果 junior workers 过去通过 first-pass work 学习，而 AI 自动化这些步骤，短期 output 可能提高，长期 expertise pipeline 却可能变弱。今天的新工具 Bottleneck Shift Test 要求先拆 workflow、找当前 constraint，再看 AI 加速哪一步、制造多少新 volume、下一处 scarcity 移到哪里，最后用真实 objective 而不是最容易统计的 proxy 衡量结果。核心问题从“How much faster is this task?”升级为“What happens to the whole system when this task becomes cheap?”。

speaking.question: Do you think AI will make most office workers much more productive?
speaking.framework: Task speed → Workflow bottlenecks → Verification → Real output
speaking.response: I think AI will make many individual tasks much faster, but the effect on overall productivity will depend on the rest of the workflow. Producing a draft may take minutes instead of hours, but someone may still need to check the facts, approve the work and coordinate implementation. In that case, the bottleneck simply moves. So I would measure productivity by useful outcomes rather than by how much content people generate. The biggest gains will probably come when organizations redesign the surrounding process instead of just adding AI to an old workflow.
expressions: The bottleneck may simply move to another stage.
I would measure productivity by useful outcomes rather than output volume.
The biggest gains require changes to the surrounding process.

speaking.question: What human skills may become more important as AI becomes more capable?
speaking.framework: Abundant generation → Scarce judgment → Verification → Context and responsibility
speaking.response: I think judgment will become more valuable because generating a plausible answer is becoming cheaper. People will still need to decide whether an answer is relevant, whether the evidence is reliable and whether an error would have serious consequences. Context also matters because the same AI output may be acceptable for brainstorming but unsafe for a high-stakes decision. So rather than saying human skills will simply disappear, I think their relative value will change: routine production may matter less, while evaluation, questioning and responsibility become more important.
expressions: Generating a plausible answer is becoming cheaper.
The relative value of human skills will change.
Evaluation and judgment become more valuable when production is abundant.
